explanation:
## Peel the digits off

```cpp
if (n < 0) n = -n;

int digits{};
int sum{};

do
{
    sum += n % 10;   // the last digit
    ++digits;
    n /= 10;         // drop it
} while (n != 0);
```

`n % 10` is the last decimal digit. `n / 10` is `n` with that digit gone,
because **integer division truncates towards zero** — `4705 / 10` is `470`, not
`470.5`. Repeat and the number shrinks a digit at a time until it reaches 0.

## Why a do-while

A plain `while (n != 0)` tests before the first pass, so an input of `0` runs
the body zero times and reports **0 digits**. But 0 is written with one digit,
so the answer is wrong for exactly one input — the kind of bug that passes every
test you thought to write.

`do { ... } while (n != 0)` tests *after* the body, so it always runs at least
once. That is the only situation where `do-while` is clearly the right loop, and
this is the canonical example of it.

The alternative is explicit and equally fine:

```cpp
if (n == 0) { std::cout << "digits 1\nsum 0\n"; return 0; }
while (n != 0) { ... }
```

Three lines instead of changing one keyword. Both are correct; the `do-while`
says "there is always at least one digit", which is the actual fact.

## Negative remainders are real

```cpp
-312 % 10   // -2 in C++, not 8
-312 / 10   // -31, truncated towards zero
```

C++ (since C++11) rounds integer division towards zero and gives the remainder
the sign of the **left** operand. Python does the opposite — `-312 % 10` is `8`
there — so a method ported from Python without thinking gives a negative digit
sum.

Taking the absolute value first sidesteps it entirely, which is why that is the
first line.

## The value the tests deliberately avoid

`INT_MIN`, which is -2,147,483,648 on a 32-bit `int`. Its absolute value is
2,147,483,648, which does **not fit in an int** — the positive range stops one
short. So `n = -n` overflows, and signed overflow is undefined behaviour: the
standard does not say you get a negative number back, it says the program has no
defined meaning, and the optimiser may assume it cannot happen.

This is not a flaw in the method; it is the asymmetry of two's complement, where
there is one more negative value than positive. Handling it properly means doing
the arithmetic in a wider type:

```cpp
long long m{ n };
if (m < 0) m = -m;      // 64 bits has room for 2147483648
```

The tests stop at `2147483647` rather than assigning a "correct" output to
something undefined.

## Why this loop keeps coming back

The same three lines convert a number to a string, compute a checksum, implement
a digital root, validate a card number with Luhn's algorithm, or print a number
in another base — change `10` to `2` and you are peeling bits. It is worth being
able to write without thinking.
